**Floating-point formats trade range, precision, and throughput.** The exponent controls how large or small a magnitude can be represented; mantissa bits control spacing between nearby values. A format can have broad range but coarse precision, or narrower range with finer relative precision. [1](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/amp_examples.html)

FP32 offers a familiar range/precision baseline. FP16 has fewer exponent bits, so very small gradients can underflow and large values can overflow. BF16 keeps an FP32-like exponent range but fewer mantissa bits, which is why it often avoids FP16's need for loss scaling while still having noticeable rounding error. TF32 is a hardware computation mode for selected FP32 operations, not simply another universally stored tensor format. FP8 has multiple formats with different range/precision tradeoffs.

**Loss scaling changes numerical representation, not the objective.** Multiply loss by a scale before backward so small gradients become representable, then divide gradients by that scale before updating. Dynamic scaling adjusts after overflow. Skipping the unscale step changes the effective update and is incorrect.

BF16's wider range reduces one failure mode, but does not guarantee all computations are safe. Reductions, optimizer states, and sensitive operations may still use higher precision. Evaluate convergence and actual kernel support; a low-bit dtype without an efficient supported kernel may save storage without delivering the expected speed.

**Technical details and references.**

FP32 has 8 exponent and 23 stored fraction bits; FP16 has 5 and 10; BF16 has 8 and 7. BF16 therefore retains FP32-like exponent range but lower precision. TF32 is a tensor-core computation mode with reduced mantissa precision, commonly using FP32 storage. FP8 formats trade still fewer exponent/fraction bits, with format-specific rules. [1](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/amp_examples.html) [3](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/)

FP16's narrow range can underflow small gradients or overflow activations. Loss scaling multiplies the loss before backward, then unscales gradients before clipping and updating. BF16 usually avoids that underflow problem because of its exponent range, but still rounds aggressively. Neither dtype guarantees stability. Keep sensitive reductions or optimizer states in adequate precision and check the actual hardware/operator implementation.
